title: Area of a Polygon (Shoelace)
description: Compute the area of any simple polygon from its vertices with the shoelace formula

blocks.text: The shoelace formula computes the area of any simple polygon directly from the coordinates of its vertices. It works for any number of sides, not just triangles and rectangles.
It is beautifully simple, runs in linear time, and as a bonus its sign tells you which way the polygon is wound.
The formula gets its name because the calculation looks like lacing a shoe: you cross multiply the coordinates of neighbouring vertices in a zig zag pattern.
Underneath, it is summing up signed areas built from cross products of consecutive vertices. Those signed pieces cancel out the parts outside the polygon and leave exactly the area inside.
Walk around the polygon vertex by vertex. For each consecutive pair, take the cross product of their coordinates, sum them all, then take half of the absolute value.

blocks.caption: Sum the cross products of consecutive vertices, then halve the absolute value

blocks.text: The vertices must be listed in order around the polygon, either all clockwise or all counter-clockwise. Out of order vertices give a wrong result.
It is a single pass, wrapping around from the last vertex back to the first.

codes.python:
def polygon_area(p):
    n = len(p)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        ax, ay = p[i]
        bx, by = p[(i + 1) % n]              # wrap around at the end
        total += ax * by - bx * ay           # cross product of the pair
    return abs(total) / 2.0

blocks.text:
Keep it exact:

The sum before halving is always an integer for integer coordinates. Keep it as an integer and only divide at the very end, so you avoid floating point error.
If you skip the absolute value, the sum has a sign, and that sign is useful on its own.

blocks.caption: The sign of the shoelace sum reveals the winding order of the vertices

items: A positive signed area means the vertices are listed counter-clockwise
A negative signed area means they are listed clockwise
Take the absolute value when you just want the area

blocks.text: This makes the shoelace formula a quick way to detect the orientation of a polygon, not only its size.
The formula is valid for any simple polygon, meaning one whose edges do not cross themselves. It handles convex and concave shapes alike, with no special casing.
The only requirement is that the vertices are given in order around the boundary. If the edges self intersect, the notion of a single area no longer makes sense, and the formula does not apply.
